Gastrointestinal Disorders

Complications of General Surgical Procedures

Postoperative patients arrive earlier in their recovery course now, so the ED has to sort expected discomfort from fever, respiratory compromise, GU obstruction, wound failure, vascular events, drug complications, and procedure-specific disasters.

Board trap: Do not anchor on “post-op fever = atelectasis”; timing, procedure type, devices, wound findings, abdomen, lungs, urine, DVT/PE, drugs, transfusion, and C. difficile all matter.

COMPLICATIONS OF GENERAL SURGICAL PROCEDURES

INTRODUCTION

The operating surgeon should be contacted when a postoperative patient appears with a complication. This is not only courtesy: it supplies operative details, expected course, implanted material, antibiotics, anatomy changes, and the threshold for reoperation.

Complications of general surgical procedures.

FEVER

Use the five Ws as a memory frame: wind, water, wound, walking, and wonder drugs. The clinical move is to combine timing with illness severity. Early fever can be atelectasis, transfusion reaction, thrombophlebitis, or severe wound infection; days 1 to 5 points toward UTI; days 3 to 7 pneumonia; days 5 to 10 wound infection; DVT/PE and drug fever can appear at variable times.

Fever without a source is not a discharge diagnosis in a fragile postoperative patient. Examine operative sites, catheter sites, lungs, abdomen, decubitus areas, and extremities, and use CBC, urinalysis/culture, chest radiography, wound culture, blood cultures, C. difficile testing when diarrhea is present, and CT/US when intra-abdominal pathology is possible.

RESPIRATORY COMPLICATIONS

ATELECTASIS

Atelectasis is alveolar collapse from retained secretions, decreased intra-alveolar pressure, anesthesia, pain, and hypoventilation. It is common after upper abdominal or thoracic surgery and may present as isolated fever, tachypnea, dyspnea, or tachycardia. Mild cases with no hypoxemia can often leave with pain control and pulmonary toilet; hypoxemia, debility, underlying lung disease, or diagnostic uncertainty requires admission.

PNEUMONIA

Postoperative pneumonia usually appears 24 to 96 hours after surgery, especially with ventilatory support or atelectasis. Symptoms include dyspnea, chest pain, productive cough, fever, and tachypnea. It is often polymicrobial; obtain sputum/blood cultures when possible and give broad parenteral coverage according to local hospital-acquired pneumonia guidance.

PNEUMOTHORAX

Pneumothorax can follow central venous access, positive-pressure ventilation, thoracic or upper abdominal procedures, breast procedures, or laparoscopy. Chest radiography may need expiratory views or CT when subtle. Management ranges from observation/needle aspiration to tube thoracostomy depending on size, symptoms, tension physiology, and ventilator use.

PULMONARY EMBOLUS

Dyspnea is the key symptom, and tachypnea, pleuritic chest pain, hypoxemia, syncope, or shock can occur. Recent surgery does not protect against PE; it raises both the risk of PE and the complexity of anticoagulation decisions. Use risk stratification, CT pulmonary angiography or V/Q scanning when indicated, and involve surgery for bleeding-risk decisions.

GU COMPLICATIONS

URINARY TRACT INFECTION

UTI becomes evident 1 to 5 days postoperatively, often related to catheterization or instrumentation. Symptoms may be absent or limited to dysuria and fever. Most stable patients can receive oral antibiotics; toxic, elderly, obstructed, or recently instrumented GU patients often need admission or urology input.

URINARY RETENTION

Retention presents with lower abdominal discomfort, urgency, and inability to void. Risk rises after anorectal surgery, longer procedures, spinal/epidural anesthesia, older age, and excess fluids. Confirm with bladder ultrasound. Rapid Foley drainage is safe; consult urology before instrumentation after GU procedures.

ACUTE RENAL FAILURE

Postoperative AKI may be prerenal from hypovolemia/bleeding/sepsis, intrinsic from nephrotoxins or ischemia, or postrenal from obstruction/retention. Evaluate volume status, urine output, electrolytes, creatinine trend, urinalysis, medication exposures, and obstruction. Most cases require admission.

WOUND COMPLICATIONS

HEMATOMAS

Hematomas arise from poor hemostasis or anticoagulation and present as swelling, pain, bruising, or drainage. Many superficial hematomas can be opened and drained, but neck hematomas, vascular-site hematomas, expanding masses, airway symptoms, or hemodynamic instability are surgical emergencies.

SEROMAS

Seromas occur in dead spaces, graft beds, axilla, groin, neck, or pelvis as painless swelling with serous aspirate. Needle aspiration confirms and relieves symptoms, but recurrence is possible.

INFECTION

Wound infection causes increasing pain, erythema, swelling, drainage, and tenderness. Clean superficial wounds may involve skin flora and be managed with drainage, culture, irrigation, packing, and outpatient antibiotics. Perineal, GI, biliary, GU, or traumatic wounds are often polymicrobial and need broad parenteral coverage and admission.

NECROTIZING FASCIITIS

Necrotizing fasciitis is the cannot-miss wound infection. Hallmarks are systemic toxicity, severe pain out of proportion, hypesthesia, crepitus, bullae, or CT gas/fluid tracking along fascia. Antibiotics must not delay immediate surgical debridement.

WOUND DEHISCENCE

Dehiscence may be superficial or fascial. Risk rises with malnutrition, glucocorticoids, diabetes, or inadequate closure. Serosanguineous drainage from abdominal wounds can warn of fascial failure. Evisceration or uncertainty about fascial integrity requires operative evaluation.

VASCULAR COMPLICATIONS

SUPERFICIAL THROMBOPHLEBITIS

Aseptic superficial thrombophlebitis presents as a red, warm, tender cord, often from venous stasis. If no cellulitis, lymphangitis, or DVT, treat with heat, elevation, and NSAIDs. Suppurative thrombophlebitis has lymphangitis/systemic features and requires excision of the vein.

DEEP VENOUS THROMBOSIS

DVT presents with leg pain, swelling, or both. Doppler ultrasound is preferred; repeat imaging is needed if symptoms persist or worsen after a normal study. Confirmed DVT usually requires admission/anticoagulation planning with the surgical bleeding risk considered.

COMPLICATIONS OF DRUG THERAPY

Anticoagulants, diabetic medications, antibiotics, and opioids are common culprits. Antibiotic-associated diarrhea can be C. difficile, even after short courses, with watery or bloody diarrhea, fever, and crampy pain. Treat by stopping the offending antibiotic when possible and using metronidazole or vancomycin by severity/local protocol. Drug fever is a diagnosis of exclusion; antibiotics are common offenders, and admission is often needed while sources are ruled out.

COMPLICATIONS OF BREAST SURGERY

Breast surgery complications are uncommon but include wound infection, hematoma, and rare pneumothorax. Hematomas often need operative control for evacuation/hemostasis. Chest symptoms after breast or axillary procedures should not be dismissed as incisional pain.

GI COMPLICATIONS

ILEUS

Adynamic ileus is expected briefly after abdominal surgery, but prolonged ileus should trigger a search for peritonitis, abscess, hemoperitoneum, pneumonia, electrolyte abnormalities, sepsis, or medication effects. Symptoms are nausea, vomiting, obstipation, constipation, distention, and pain. CT helps distinguish functional ileus from mechanical obstruction and ischemia.

INTRA-ABDOMINAL ABSCESS

Abscess follows preoperative contamination, bowel-content spillage, contaminated hematoma, or anastomotic leak. Fever, chills, anorexia, abdominal tenderness, ileus, and leukocytosis may be nonspecific. CT or US is diagnostic; treatment is broad antibiotics plus percutaneous drainage or surgery.

PANCREATITIS

Postoperative pancreatitis follows pancreatic manipulation or retraction, gastric resection, biliary surgery, or ERCP. Look for nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, leukocytosis, pleural effusion, Turner/Cullen signs, and elevated lipase. Treatment parallels nonoperative pancreatitis while searching for complications.

CHOLECYSTITIS

Biliary colic, calculous cholecystitis, and acalculous cholecystitis can occur after surgery. Acalculous disease can be occult, especially in older or critically ill patients. Ultrasound findings include enlarged gallbladder, wall thickening, and pericholecystic fluid without stones; early intervention reduces morbidity.

FISTULAS

Enterocutaneous fistulas can occur anywhere in the GI tract from technical complication or bowel injury. High-output proximal fistulas cause volume depletion and electrolyte loss; sepsis is the other major danger. Most require admission, although many eventually close.

TETANUS

Tetanus has been reported after general surgery, particularly GI surgery where C. tetani may contaminate devitalized tissue, clots, or sutures. Initial signs may be abdominal discomfort, fever, and abdominal wall rigidity before classic trismus/opisthotonos. Check immunization and treat early when suspected.

ANASTOMOTIC LEAKS

Leaks are most common after esophageal and colonic anastomoses. Esophageal leaks can cause fever, chest pain, tachypnea, tachycardia, shock, pneumothorax, or pleural effusion; gastric leaks may cause pain, fever, leukocytosis, obstruction, hyperamylasemia, hyperbilirubinemia, peritonitis, or shock. Resuscitation, broad antibiotics, nasogastric drainage, contrast imaging/CT, and urgent surgical involvement are the ED sequence.

GASTRIC SURGERY

GASTRIC BYPASS

Early post-bypass abdominal pain, tachycardia, fever, tenderness, hypotension, or vomiting should trigger concern for anastomotic leak or intra-abdominal bleeding, even if imaging is imperfect. Later complications include bowel obstruction, stomal stenosis/ulcer/obstruction, cholelithiasis, dumping syndrome, and vitamin deficiency. Any cerebellar signs, ophthalmoplegia, weakness, or memory change after bariatric surgery is Wernicke until treated with thiamine.

Complications of gastric bypass procedures.

NONBARIATRIC GASTRIC SURGERY

Partial or complete gastrectomy can lead to dumping syndrome, alkaline reflux gastritis, afferent loop syndrome, and postvagotomy diarrhea. Afferent loop syndrome causes severe epigastric pain 1 to 2 hours after eating, relieved by bilious vomiting, and requires contrast/endoscopic diagnosis and operative reconstruction.

LAPAROSCOPIC SURGERY

BILIARY TRACT SURGERY

Most cholecystectomies are laparoscopic. Postoperative pain with fever or peritoneal signs suggests biliary injury or leak. CT may show bile collection, but ERCP often localizes injury and treats retained stones or strictures. Spilled gallstones can later cause abscess, fistula, pelvic pain, or infertility-related ovarian implantation.

Complications of cholecystectomy.

OTHER LAPAROSCOPIC SURGERIES

Laparoscopy can complicate appendectomy, colectomy, antireflux surgery, herniorrhaphy, fundoplication, gynecologic, and urologic procedures. Risks come from pneumoperitoneum and trocar/needle insertion: arrhythmia, subcutaneous emphysema, pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, CO2 embolism, bleeding, bowel/GU/major vessel injury, trocar hernia, and wound infection.

Tintinalli source

Table 87-6

Complications of laparoscopy.

STOMAS

Ileostomy and colostomy problems include technical complications, Crohn disease or carcinoma at the stoma, ischemia/necrosis, peristomal irritation, hernia, and prolapse. A healthy stoma is pink and painless. Cyanosis, necrosis, incarceration, obstruction, or viability concerns require surgical evaluation.

COLONOSCOPY

Colonoscopy complications include hemorrhage, perforation, retroperitoneal abscess, pneumoscrotum, pneumothorax, volvulus, distention, splenic rupture, appendicitis, bacteremia, and infection. Intraluminal bleeding presents as rectal bleeding; mesenteric or splenic injury presents as intra-abdominal bleeding. Perforation usually needs laparotomy, although select late stable patients without peritonitis may be observed in hospital.

RECTAL SURGERY

After hemorrhoidectomy, urinary retention is common; constipation is treated gently with rectal exam only when appropriate, disimpaction if present, and enemas when safe. Posthemorrhoidectomy hemorrhage can be immediate or delayed and may be massive; Foley balloon tamponade can temporize until surgical ligation. Rectal prolapse needs reduction and surgical consultation. Infection is uncommon but increasing pain/fever requires exam for abscess, cellulitis, or Fournier gangrene.

Anorectal Necrotizing Infection

Rosen anorectal chapter cross-check for Fournier/necrotizing infection after anorectal infection.
